c.tagline: Red-tiled valleys beneath the Ávila, guarded and grand.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are rarely used; agree on a price (often in USD) with the driver before departing.

emergency.note: 171 is the national emergency dispatch line covering police, fire, and ambulance; CICPC (investigative police) can also be reached directly for crime reporting. English-speaking operators are rare, so ask hotel staff for help if needed.

avoid.reason: Avoid the hillside barrios entirely — Petare, Catia, 23 de Enero, El Valle and similar — where violent crime is severe even by day.
Even in safer Chacao, Altamira and Las Mercedes, phone snatching and express kidnappings occur — don't display valuables, use trusted drivers, and avoid the airport road after dark.

hood_desc: Leafy, upscale residential district with plazas, cafes and a Metro station; popular with business travelers and families wanting a quieter, well-guarded base.
Caracas's main dining and nightlife district, packed with restaurants, bars and shopping malls; suits visitors who want to be at the center of the action after dark.
A polished mid-town area of high-rises, embassies and international hotels near the CCCT mall; good for business travelers wanting a central, relatively calm location.
A compact financial and hotel district wedged between Chacaíto and Las Mercedes, walkable to bars and offices; suits travelers who prioritize convenience over sightseeing.
A historic, lively pedestrian boulevard near Plaza Venezuela with budget lodging and street life; suits budget travelers and those wanting a slice of everyday Caracas.

water.note: Tap water is unreliable and unsafe for visitors; drink bottled water.

transit.pay: Metro fares are paid with a rechargeable magnetic or contactless card sold and topped up at station booths; cash is not accepted directly at turnstiles. Buses, Metrobús and por puesto shared vans are paid in cash (bolívares, and increasingly USD) directly to the driver.
transit.hours: Metro runs roughly 5:30 AM to 11 PM daily with no all-night service; late-night travelers rely on taxis or ride-hailing apps.
transit.note: Fares are heavily subsidized and very cheap in USD terms, but overcrowding, occasional breakdowns and long queues are common.

food.name: Arepas
food.desc: Griddled maize cakes split and stuffed to order; reina pepiada (chicken and avocado) and pelua (beef and cheese) are the Caracas classics.

places.name: Arepera La Coriana
places.note: Fast counter service and a huge filling list; the reina pepiada is the one regulars order.

places.name: Arepazo
places.note: Polished arepera with dozens of fillings, popular with families and open late.

places.name: El Budare
places.note: Long-running criollo kitchen where arepas come alongside full plated Venezuelan food.

food.name: Pabellon criollo
food.desc: Venezuela's national plate: shredded stewed beef, black beans, white rice and sweet fried plantain, sometimes topped with a fried egg.

places.name: La Cocina de Francy
places.note: Beloved neighbourhood kitchen whose pabellon is the dish people travel across town for.

places.name: El Budare
places.note: Reliable, generous version with tajadas and a fried egg on request.

places.name: Mercado de Chacao
places.note: Upstairs market comedores serve pabellon at lunch to office workers at everyday prices.

food.name: Cachapa
food.desc: A thick, sweet pancake of fresh young corn folded over soft queso de mano, butter melting out of the edges.

places.name: El Budare
places.note: Cachapa con queso de mano is a fixture of the menu and reliably well made.

places.name: Arepazo
places.note: Serves cachapas alongside the arepas, with pork or cheese fillings.

places.name: Mercado de Chacao
places.note: Market stalls griddle them to order in the morning, cheaper than the restaurants.

food.name: Tequenos
food.desc: Batons of salty white cheese wrapped in thin dough and deep-fried; the country's universal party snack, eaten by the dozen.

places.name: Mercado de Chacao
places.note: Bakery counters fry them in batches through the day; buy a bag hot.

places.name: Arepera La Coriana
places.note: Solid tequenos as a starter or a quick standing snack with a fruit juice.

places.name: Panaderias of Sabana Grande
places.note: Neighbourhood bakeries turn them out all morning alongside coffee and pastries.

food.name: Cachito de jamon
food.desc: A soft crescent bread roll baked around chopped ham, the standard Caracas breakfast taken standing at a bakery counter.

places.name: Panaderias of Sabana Grande
places.note: Portuguese-founded bakeries here are the heart of the cachito-and-coffee ritual.

places.name: Mercado de Chacao
places.note: Bakery stalls sell cachitos and pastelitos from early morning.

food.name: Hallaca
food.desc: Christmas-season parcel of maize dough filled with a stew of beef, pork, olives and capers, tied in plantain leaves and steamed.

places.name: Mercado de Chacao
places.note: From November onward stalls sell homemade hallacas by the dozen; the best sell out early.

places.name: La Cocina de Francy
places.note: Puts hallacas and pan de jamon on the menu through the festive season.

food.name: Papelon con limon
food.desc: Unrefined cane sugar dissolved in water with lime and plenty of ice; tart, molasses-scented and the standard drink with an arepa.

places.name: Arepera La Coriana
places.note: Poured by the jug alongside the arepas, cheaper and better than bottled soft drinks.

places.name: Mercado de Chacao
places.note: Juice counters mix it fresh with batidos of mango, parchita and guanabana.

places.name: El Budare
places.note: Served in tall glasses with criollo lunches.

food.name: Cafe marron and guayoyo
food.desc: Venezuelan coffee ordered by shade: guayoyo is long and black, marroncito a small milky cut, negrito a straight espresso.

places.name: Panaderias of Sabana Grande
places.note: The classic setting for a standing marron with a cachito, any time of day.

places.name: Mercado de Chacao
places.note: Coffee counters inside the market pour for traders from dawn.

landmarks: Cerro El Ávila (Waraira Repano)
The forested mountain wall that separates Caracas from the Caribbean coast, offering the city's most dramatic backdrop and panoramic viewpoints.
Teleférico Warairarepano (Mount Ávila Cable Car)
A historic cable car climbing from the city up to the summit of Ávila, delivering sweeping views of Caracas and the sea beyond.
Plaza Bolívar de Caracas
The colonial-era heart of the city, anchored by an equestrian statue of Simón Bolívar and ringed by historic institutions.
Catedral de Caracas
An 18th-century cathedral on Plaza Bolívar with a striking baroque facade and the tomb of Bolívar's family.
Capitolio Nacional
The seat of Venezuela's legislature, crowned by a gilded dome and lavishly muraled Elliptical Hall depicting the independence wars.
Panteón Nacional
A grand neoclassical mausoleum honoring Bolívar and Venezuela's national heroes, one of the country's most solemn and photogenic monuments.
Aula Magna, Universidad Central de Venezuela
A UNESCO World Heritage modernist masterpiece by Carlos Raúl Villanueva, famed for its floating Alexander Calder acoustic sculptures.
Teatro Teresa Carreño
Caracas's premier performing-arts complex, a bold Brutalist landmark that is a hub of the city's cultural life.
Torres de El Silencio
Twin Art Deco towers marking the historic El Silencio district, one of Caracas's most recognizable urban renewal landmarks.
Parque del Este (Parque Generalísimo Francisco de Miranda)
A sprawling green oasis designed by Roberto Burle Marx, home to lakes, a planetarium, and abundant wildlife in the middle of the city.

dom.op: IFE (Instituto de Ferrocarriles del Estado) — tickets at the station, no online booking

train.note: No international trains. The only passenger line serving the capital is the suburban Caracas-Cúa route (Ezequiel Zamora system) operated by state railway IFE; tickets are sold at the stations and there is no reliable online booking. There is no long-distance intercity rail.

bus.note: There are no dependable scheduled international coaches from Caracas right now. For Colombia, travelers take a domestic bus from Terminal La Bandera toward San Cristóbal and cross on foot at San Antonio del Táchira / Cúcuta; for Brazil, buses head east toward Santa Elena de Uairén. Carry your passport and check current border and security conditions before setting out.

ferry.note: No international passenger ferries from Caracas. Domestic ferries to Isla Margarita (operators such as Conferry and Navibus) sail from La Guaira and Puerto La Cruz rather than the city itself, and the old ferry link to Trinidad is not running.
